introduction: These eighty-nine passages, nearly all from ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, make one claim from many sides: nothing exists alone. The universe is a body whose members help one another, a chain in which no link can be struck without the rest feeling it, a traffic of atoms through mineral, plant, animal and human, so that “all things are involved in all things”. From this he draws answers to questions about fate, earthquakes, astrology and war. The guide is given whole, and beside it stand as many voices from elsewhere: Paul’s body and its members, the Qur’an’s creation without a rift, Marcus Aurelius and Pope on the chain, Hamlet in the graveyard, Whitman’s atoms, Darwin’s entangled bank, and Voltaire after Lisbon, who would not be consoled by any talk of the whole. Most stand close to the reading they follow; those that differ or add end in a question.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá sees co-operation as the foundation of existence; Tennyson and Darwin saw struggle in the same fields, and Adam Smith saw self-interest. Describe one piece of the living world you know well. Which account fits it?

Asked whether an earthquake was caused by wickedness, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answers from the connection of things, as Jesus did of the tower in Siloam. Voltaire found such answers cold. What would you say to someone who had lost a home?
Fate is defined here as the necessary relationships between things. Set that beside Cassius, Khayyám and the sparrow of the Gospel. How much room does each leave for what a person decides?
The atoms of a flower become an animal, a person, a stone. Hamlet, Whitman, the Preacher and Lucretius all knew this. Why does the same fact console one and unsettle another?
The ocean’s atoms keep their identity, says one reading; the rivers of the Upanishad forget their names. Which picture of belonging to a whole would you rather were true, and why?
“If the people should understand this aright, they would never war.” Marcus Aurelius understood it and fought for years. What has to be added to understanding?

outside.why: The world of being is likened to a single tree, its peoples to leaves, blossoms and fruit. Jesus uses the same figure for those who follow him: I am the vine, ye are the branches.
From the interconnection of the world-tree ‘Abdu’l-Bahá draws a duty of kindness to one’s fellows. Sa‘dí drew the same duty from the same fact: the sons of Adam are limbs of each other.
“No atom can succeed without help and assistance.” Emerson put it in two lines of a poem about a sparrow, a shell and a bride: all are needed by each one.

If help ceased “for the twinkling of an eye”, the living being would cease to exist. The Psalmist says of every creature: thou hidest thy face, they are troubled; thou takest away their breath, they die.
“The greatest foundation of the world of existence is this co-operation and mutuality.” Kropotkin, a naturalist writing in the same years, read the same lesson in the animals of Siberia.
All existing things “are linked together and draw help from each other”. Marcus Aurelius wrote it in his notebook on campaign: all things are implicated with one another, and the bond is holy.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá sees co-operation growing more conspicuous as creation rises from mineral to plant to animal. Tennyson, looking at the same animal world, saw Nature red in tooth and claw. Which of them is describing what a naturalist finds?

Reciprocity, the tablet says, is plainer in each higher kingdom. Darwin’s entangled bank shows plants, birds, insects and worms “dependent on each other in so complex a manner”, and all of it produced by struggle. Can co-operation and struggle be one fact seen from two sides?
“The world of existence is like the human form”, all its members assisting one another. Paul works the figure out limb by limb: if the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body.
Each stone of a building depends on the others, and one faulty stone leaves the structure imperfect. Paul says the same of a body “fitly joined together” by what every joint supplies.
“If one were displaced the whole building would suffer.” Pope says it of a chain: strike any link, tenth or ten thousandth, and the chain is broken alike.

All the members of this endless universe are linked “even as are the members of the human body”. Marcus Aurelius told himself to regard the universe constantly as one living being, with one substance and one soul.
“Every single thing has an effect and influence upon every other.” Muir found it in the Sierra: try to pick out anything by itself and it is hitched to everything else in the universe.
All beings “are linked together like a chain”. Donne heard it in a funeral bell: no man is an island, and any man’s death diminishes me.

Mutual aid, in this tablet, is an intrinsic property of beings. Adam Smith agreed that we need one another at all times and found the link in self-interest, not benevolence. Is help that is given for one’s own advantage still mutual aid?
The parts of the universe “mutually assist, reinforce and influence each other” like the organs of a body. Paul’s form of it: whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it.
“This endless universe is like the human body.” Pope gave the image its best-known English couplet: all are but parts of one stupendous whole.
Created things are connected “through essential relationships which are a divine trust”. King wrote from a jail cell of an inescapable network of mutuality, a single garment of destiny.

Every being “hath come to exist under numerous influences”, themselves formed by others. The Tao Te Ching tells the same descent in numbers: the One produced Two, Two produced Three, Three produced all things.

The mind follows cause behind cause, while the Universal Reality stays “exalted above all minds”. The voice from the whirlwind stops Job at the same place: where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?

Fate, here, is the necessary relationships in the realities of things, and will the force that governs them. Cassius gives will all the room: the fault is not in our stars, but in ourselves. How much of what happens to a person does each account leave to that person?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá defines predestination as relationships like that of sun and soil, and leaves will its part. Khayyám’s Moving Finger writes, and no piety or wit can cancel half a line. Is an order of relationships the same thing as a sentence already written?
“Every matter is connected to all matters”, and those connections are the divine destinies. Paul’s confidence rests on the same linkage: all things work together for good.
“A link cannot be broken without affecting that natural order.” Jesus takes the smallest link he can find: one sparrow shall not fall on the ground without your Father.
Everything that happens “is in conformity with this order and is based on consummate wisdom”. Pope’s lines are the classic statement: all discord, harmony not understood; whatever is, is right.

The chain of creation, on this account, is interwoven in consummate wisdom. Voltaire, after Lisbon, turned on that very thought: you would compose a general bliss from individuals’ woes? What does the sufferer hear when told that everything is linked?

Asked whether flood and earthquake are caused by wickedness, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answers from the connection of things. Jesus was asked the same about a fallen tower: think ye that they were sinners above all men? I tell you, Nay.

Events like the San Francisco earthquake “happen because of the connection between the parts of the universe”. Voltaire had put the question behind the question after the Lisbon earthquake: was there more vice there than in Paris?
“Even seemingly small occurrences are part of this divine plan.” The Qur’an makes the occurrence as small as it can be: not a leaf falleth but He knoweth it.
“The stars in the sky do not exert any spiritual influence on this world of dust.” Edmund in King Lear says so with more scorn: we make guilty of our disasters the sun, the moon, and the stars.

The tablet denies the stars a spiritual influence and grants them a material one. Job is asked whether he can bind “the sweet influences of Pleiades” or set heaven’s dominion in the earth. What kind of influence is that question about?
“The words of the astrologers are for the most part doubtful and unreliable.” Isaiah taunts Babylon with them: let the stargazers and monthly prognosticators stand up and save thee.

Kepler and Newton, the talk says, discovered “a universal law of interdependence between the stars”. Newton himself read that order as contrivance: we know God only by his most wise and excellent contrivances of things.
Because all beings are members of one body, “from any part … the realities of other parts can be discovered”. Blake’s lines claim as much: a world in a grain of sand.
From any one part the others can be known. Tennyson holds a flower pulled from a wall and says that to understand it, root and all, would be to know what God and man is.

The elements of a man decompose and become “part of a flower … or part of a stone”. Hamlet follows them in a graveyard: imperious Caesar, dead and turned to clay, might stop a hole to keep the wind away.
Man “is created by the gathering of single elements”, which do not stay. Genesis says it in eight words: dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
“Every particle of creation compriseth all creation.” Whitman begins his long poem from the same physics: every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you.
“All created things exist in all created things.” Leibniz reached it by argument: each simple substance, related to all the others, is a perpetual living mirror of the universe.

The element’s journey through all things is here a proof of unity. The Preacher sees the same journey and draws no comfort from it: all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again. What makes one reader find unity there and another vanity?
All existing things “pass through the same degrees and phases”, and any one embodies the others. Heraclitus left a sentence for it: the way up and the way down is one and the same.
The atom passes “through endless forms and stages”, with virtues peculiar to each. Rúmí tells that passage in the first person: I died as mineral and became a plant.
“Every thing is connected to every other thing”, and each atom gathers perfections as it goes. Whitman: a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars.

One primordial atom has travelled through every stage of life and been given a virtue in each. The Gita says something like it of the spirit, which lays aside worn-out robes and takes new ones. Does it matter whether what travels is an atom or a self?
What is flower now may be animal later. Thoreau asks it of himself at Walden: am I not partly leaves and vegetable mould myself?
Without these passages across the kingdoms “the chain of being would be broken”. Pope gave English the phrase: vast chain of being, from infinite to thee, from thee to nothing.

Motion through the realms keeps “the innate order of nature”. Shakespeare’s Ulysses says order depends on each thing keeping its degree: untune that string, and hark what discord follows. Is the order of nature kept by movement or by staying in place?
The body’s dispersal should be gradual, so that the chain of transferences is not broken. Whitman makes his own will in those terms: I bequeath myself to the dirt to grow from the grass I love.
“All creatures are eaters and eaten, and the very fabric of life is reared upon this fact.” Hamlet shocks a king with it: a man may fish with the worm that hath eat of a king.
The ties of the universe “admit of no imbalance, nor any slackening whatever”. The Qur’an challenges the eye to find one: look again, canst thou see any rift?
“The death of one confers life upon another.” Jesus says it of a grain: except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone.
Grass lost in outward form “has gone into the make-up of a higher life”. Paul argues from the same field: that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die.
Animals breathe out what plants live on, and plants give back what animals live on. Job tells his friends where to learn such things: ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee.
“All are connected by the bond of existence. What greater bond is there than this?” Paul named it to the Athenians with a line from their own poets: in him we live, and move, and have our being.
The world of existence is “as one person”, its members working together. Paul’s phrase for a community that knows this: every one members one of another.
In physical respects “the selfsame feelings are shared by animal and man”. The Qur’an calls every beast and bird peoples like unto you.
Animal and man share the same feelings. Coleridge’s mariner learned at sea what follows from that: he prayeth best, who loveth best all things both great and small.

Creation is hierarchical here, and “animals can never aspire to gain rational faculties”. Darwin closes his book with endless forms evolved from so simple a beginning. Can both be held, a fixed ladder of kingdoms and forms that have climbed it?
The kingdoms form “an endless chain of existence”, each merging imperceptibly into the next. Milton’s angel describes it to Adam as one first matter, more refined the nearer it is placed to God.
“Can man imagine that the endless chain is broken with him?” Whitman, looking at grass on graves, answers no: all goes onward and outward, nothing collapses.

The chain of life, the talk implies, does not end with man’s death. Lucretius reasoned from the same atoms to the opposite: when we are no more, nothing whatever can happen to us. What in the idea of a chain decides between them?

Asked what “Everything is in everything” means, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of every particle transformed into all forms. The Qur’an says that the creation and raising of all mankind is as that of a single soul.

The atoms of an ocean are the ocean in appearance, “but the identity of the atoms remains”. The Chandogya Upanishad’s rivers reach the sea and no longer know which river they were. Is individuality kept or surrendered when the part joins the whole?
Individuality remains within the ocean of life. Shelley’s lines hold the One and the many differently: the One remains, the many change and pass. What does each image let a person hope for?
“There is an invisible chain binding all into one.” Coleridge felt it one evening by a window: the one Life within us and abroad, which meets all motion and becomes its soul.
The machines of a factory all turn by one power, and so creation has “a moving force which is the axis and mover”. Dante ends his poem there: the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
The interaction of created things is “connected to a moving power”. Wordsworth, above the Wye, felt a motion and a spirit that impels all thinking things and rolls through all things.
Earthly and heavenly, material and spiritual, “are connected one with another”. Jacob dreamed the connection as a ladder set up on the earth, its top reaching to heaven.
“Physical things are signs and imprints of spiritual things.” Paul says the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
The material world “has an outward appearance, as it has also an inner reality”. Hebrews: things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.

Created things are linked in a chain “ultimately ending in abstract realities”. Plato’s prisoners take the shadows on the wall for the whole of what is. How would one know, from inside, that there is a further link?
“A spiritual connection exists between the thought of man and that outward form.” Emerson finds the evidence in language: every word for a fact of mind is borrowed from some material appearance.

When man looks at plain or mountain “there is a wave of spiritual communication between the two”. Wordsworth believed it enough to say one impulse from a vernal wood could teach more than all the sages.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says a current passes between man and meadow though no word is spoken. To Peter Bell a primrose was a yellow primrose, and it was nothing more. Is the communication in the meadow or in the one who looks?
Lover and beloved, light and eye, cloud and land, breeze and tree: “this process is found in all things”. Shelley’s love poem argues the same way: nothing in the world is single.
All things communicate, as the sun with the earth. The Psalm hears it as speech without words: day unto day uttereth speech, and their voice is not heard.
Creation is like letters, and “Christ’s station is that of the Word, which has complete and independent meaning”. This is John’s sentence on which the talk comments.
The reader is to observe “all the signs in the universe in every atom”. Hopkins saw it so: the world is charged with the grandeur of God; it will flame out, like shining from shook foil.
The signs are to be witnessed “within thine inmost being” and in the universe. The tablet echoes this verse of the Qur’an: portents on the horizons and within themselves.
In one station unity “is sanctified above description and utterance”. The Tao Te Ching opens with the same reserve: the name that can be named is not the enduring name.

“All the saplings of the world have appeared from one Tree … and all beings owe their existence to one Being.” The verse of Kabir in the Sikh scripture: from the one Light the whole universe welled up.
All drops are from one Ocean. Paul told Athens that God made of one blood all nations of men.

Union and association are “the cause of life for all beings”, separation their death. Heraclitus saw life in the flowing apart as well: fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you. Is dissolution only death, or also the way the elements move on?
“We are the waves of one sea and the drops of one river.” Schiller’s ode, which Beethoven set to music, says it of all mankind under one joy.

From the height the freed soul sees “every atom of existence breathing life and force”. The Qur’an hears the same scene: there is not a thing but hymneth His praise, though ye understand not their praise.
Bahá’u’lláh quotes this verse and explains it: since all that is in the world exists in a single soul, to give life to one is to give life to all. Here is the verse in full.
The Qur’an says this was decreed for the Children of Israel. The Mishnah has the teaching in its own words and gives its own reason: a single person was created first.
If people understood the oneness of existence aright, “they would never war”. Aesop taught the practical half to children with a bundle of sticks.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá expects that understanding oneness would end war. Marcus Aurelius understood it, called acting against one another contrary to nature, and spent his reign at war. What more than understanding is needed?

luke-tower-in-siloam.text: Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish

john-who-did-sin.text: And as Jesus passed by, he saw a man which was blind from his birth. And his disciples asked him, saying, Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind? Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him

matthew-rain-on-the-just.text: That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust

matthew-sparrow-shall-not-fall.text: Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows

corinthians-one-body-many-members.text: For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ

corinthians-if-the-foot-shall-say.text: For the body is not one member, but many. If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body? And if the ear shall say, Because I am not the eye, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing? If the whole were hearing, where were the smelling? But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him

romans-members-one-of-another.text: For as we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office: So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another

ephesians-fitly-joined-together.text: From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love

john-vine-and-branches.text: I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing

acts-live-and-move.text: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring

genesis-dust-thou-art.text: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return

ecclesiastes-all-are-of-the-dust.text: All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again

psalm-these-wait-all-upon-thee.text: These wait all upon thee; that thou mayest give them their meat in due season. That thou givest them they gather: thou openest thine hand, they are filled with good. Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled: thou takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust. Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth

job-ask-now-the-beasts.text: But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee: Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee. Who knoweth not in all these that the hand of the Lord hath wrought this? In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind

jeremiah-signs-of-heaven.text: Thus saith the Lord, Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them

isaiah-astrologers.text: Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee

ecclesiastes-rivers-run-into-the-sea.text: All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again

corinthians-not-quickened-except-it-die.text: Thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die: And that which thou sowest, thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain, it may chance of wheat, or of some other grain: But God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body

psalm-praise-him-sun-and-moon.text: Praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, all ye stars of light. Praise him, ye heavens of heavens, and ye waters that be above the heavens. Let them praise the name of the Lord: for he commanded, and they were created

isaiah-all-flesh-is-grass.text: The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the Lord bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever

judges-stars-in-their-courses.text: They fought from heaven; the stars in their courses fought against Sisera

job-sweet-influences-of-pleiades.text: Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion? Canst thou bring forth Mazzaroth in his season? or canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons? Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? canst thou set the dominion thereof in the earth

quran-whoso-slew-a-soul.text: For that cause We decreed for the Children of Israel that whosoever killeth a human being for other than manslaughter or corruption in the earth, it shall be as if he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind. Our messengers came unto them of old with clear proofs (of Allah's Sovereignty), but afterwards lo! many of them became prodigals in the earth.

quran-communities-like-unto-you.text: There is not an animal in the earth, nor a flying creature flying on two wings, but they are peoples like unto you. We have neglected nothing in the Book (of Our decrees). Then unto their Lord they will be gathered.

quran-not-a-leaf-falleth.text: And with Him are the keys of the Invisible. None but He knoweth them. And He knoweth what is in the land and the sea. Not a leaf falleth but He knoweth it, not a grain amid the darkness of the earth, naught of wet or dry but (it is noted) in a clear record.

quran-hymneth-his-praise.text: The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein praise Him, and there is not a thing but hymneth His praise; but ye understand not their praise. Lo! He is ever Clement, Forgiving.

quran-heavens-and-earth-of-one-piece.text: Have not those who disbelieve known that the heavens and the earth were of one piece, then We parted them, and we made every living thing of water? Will they not then believe?

quran-each-knoweth-its-worship.text: Hast thou not seen that Allah, He it is Whom all who are in the heavens and the earth praise, and the birds in their flight? Of each He knoweth verily the worship and the praise; and Allah is Aware of what they do.

quran-all-things-in-pairs.text: Glory be to Him Who created all the sexual pairs, of that which the earth groweth, and of themselves, and of that which they know not!

quran-created-by-measure.text: Lo! We have created every thing by measure.

quran-as-a-single-soul.text: Your creation and your raising (from the dead) are only as (the creation and the raising of) a single soul. Lo! Allah is Hearer, Knower.

quran-stars-to-guide.text: And He it is Who hath set for you the stars that ye may guide your course by them amid the darkness of the land and the sea. We have detailed Our revelations for a people who have knowledge.

mishnah-single-soul.text: Therefore but a single person was created in the world, to teach that if any man has caused a single life to perish from Israel, he is deemed by Scripture as if he had caused a whole world to perish; and anyone who saves a single soul from Israel, he is deemed by Scripture as if he had saved a whole world

marcus-bond-is-holy.author: Marcus Aurelius

marcus-one-living-being.text: Constantly regard the universe as one living being, having one substance and one soul; and observe how all things have reference to one perception, the perception of this one living being; and how all things act with one movement
marcus-one-living-being.author: Marcus Aurelius

dante-love-which-moves-the-sun.text: But now was turning my desire and will, / Even as a wheel that equally is moved, / The Love which moves the sun and the other stars
dante-love-which-moves-the-sun.author: Dante Alighieri

shakespeare-imperious-caesar.author: William Shakespeare

shakespeare-untune-that-string.author: William Shakespeare

emerson-each-and-all.text: All are needed by each one; / Nothing is fair or good alone
emerson-each-and-all.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

shelley-nothing-is-single.text: The fountains mingle with the river / And the rivers with the Ocean, / The winds of Heaven mix for ever / With a sweet emotion; / Nothing in the world is single; 5 / All things by a law divine / In one spirit meet and mingle. / Why not I with thine
shelley-nothing-is-single.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

coleridge-one-life.text: O! the one Life, within us and abroad, / Which meets all Motion, and becomes its soul, / A Light in Sound, a sound-like power in Light, / Rhythm in all Thought, and Joyance every where
coleridge-one-life.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge

wordsworth-rolls-through-all-things.text: And I have felt / A presence that disturbs me with the joy / Of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime / Of something far more deeply interfused, / Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, / And the round ocean and the living air, / And the blue sky, and in the mind of man: / A motion and a spirit, that impels / All thinking things, all objects of all thought, / And rolls through all things
wordsworth-rolls-through-all-things.author: William Wordsworth
wordsworth-rolls-through-all-things.work: Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey

whitman-journey-work-of-the-stars.text: I believe a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars, / And the pismire is equally perfect, and a grain of sand, and the egg of the wren
whitman-journey-work-of-the-stars.author: Walt Whitman

whitman-under-your-boot-soles.text: I bequeath myself to the dirt to grow from the grass I love, / If you want me again look for me under your boot-soles
whitman-under-your-boot-soles.author: Walt Whitman

leibniz-living-mirror.text: Now this connexion or adaptation of all created things to each and of each to all, means that each simple substance has relations which express all the others, and, consequently, that it is a perpetual living mirror of the universe
leibniz-living-mirror.author: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz

thoreau-vegetable-mould.text: Shall I not have intelligence with the earth? Am I not partly leaves and vegetable mould myself
thoreau-vegetable-mould.author: Henry David Thoreau

darwin-entangled-bank.text: It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth, and to reflect that these elaborately constructed forms, so different from each other, and dependent on each other in so complex a manner, have all been produced by laws acting around us
darwin-entangled-bank.author: Charles Darwin

shakespeare-excellent-foppery.text: This is the excellent foppery of the world, that, when we are sick in fortune,—often the surfeit of our own behavior,—we make guilty of our disasters the sun, the moon, and the stars: as if we were villains by necessity; fools by heavenly compulsion
shakespeare-excellent-foppery.author: William Shakespeare

voltaire-general-bliss.text: Thus the world's members equal ills sustain, / And perish by each other born to pain: / Yet in this direful chaos you'd compose / A general bliss from individuals' woes?
voltaire-general-bliss.author: Voltaire

pope-chain-of-being.text: From nature's chain whatever link you strike, / Tenth, or ten thousandth, breaks the chain alike
pope-chain-of-being.author: Alexander Pope

pope-stupendous-whole.text: All are but parts of one stupendous whole, / Whose body nature is and God the soul
pope-stupendous-whole.author: Alexander Pope

pope-vast-chain.text: Vast chain of being, which from God began, / Natures ethereal, human, angel, man, / Beast, bird, fish, insect! what no Eye can see, / No glass can reach! from infinite to thee, / From thee to nothing
pope-vast-chain.author: Alexander Pope
